The cloak is designed using a linear homogeneous coordinate transformation method.
The polygonal cloak divides the cloak region into triangular segments with homogeneous anisotropic materials.
A simplified hexagonal cloak was fabricated using six calcite trapezoids glued together.
Calcite has refractive indices of 1.66 (ordinary) and 1.49 (extraordinary) light.
The cloak works for six incident directions corresponding to the hexagonal symmetry.
The inner radius of the cloak is 1.5 mm, outer radius 13 cm, and height 13 mm.
The cloak hides a yellow cylindrical object with radius 1.3 mm immersed in a liquid of refractive index 1.72.
The cloak guides visible light rays around the hidden object without distortion or shadow.
The experimental setup used a camera to capture images through the cloak to validate invisibility.
The simplified cloak sacrifices omnidirectional cloaking performance by removing highly anisotropic materials.
Theoretical analysis shows the polygonal cloak can render an object invisible from all directions.
The cloak does not require a reflective ground plane, unlike carpet cloaks.
Laser beams at 561 nm and 650 nm wavelengths were used to demonstrate cloaking at oblique incidence.
The cloak's electromagnetic parameters are finite and spatially independent.
The cloak is a step toward feasible human cloaking devices in visible light.
The linear homogeneous transformation avoids extreme material parameters required in earlier designs.
The cloak's design can be extended to other polygonal shapes and optical devices.
The six trapezoidal calcite pieces have optic axes perpendicular to their sides.
Small fabrication gaps cause minor image artifacts but do not affect overall cloaking performance.
The cloak experimentally demonstrates broadband operation across the visible spectrum.
